case_studies.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
case_studies.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
case_studies.summary: SwarmEvolve tackles slow evolutionary AI searches by deploying many low-cost agents that reason in latent space, avoiding long text generation. It builds a swarm framework that shares key‑value caches, filters novelty, and merges ideas naturally, achieving top scores on scientific problems in minutes rather than hours. This research is not directly relevant to typical cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a novel latent-agent swarm approach for evolutionary search, which could theoretically speed up program optimization tasks. However, its applicability to everyday IT engineering tasks (e.g., infrastructure management, SaaS tooling, DevOps automation) is indirect and speculative. No released code or deployment examples are provided, and the system is still a research prototype. Consequently, immediate practical use or monetisation within 90 days is unlikely.

case_studies.title: Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: We study zero-shot coordination (ZSC), where independently developed agents must coordinate at test time. While ZSC has been well studied in the RL literature, far less is known about the performance of LLM agents despite their increasing deployment in such settings. Existing work on LLM coordination often relies on specialised scaffolding that independently developed agents are unlikely to share in practice. Moreover, evaluations on complex environments (e.g., Hanabi) make it difficult to pinpoint the sources of coordination failure. In contrast, we focus on simple, general-purpose scaffolds in minimal environments designed to isolate specific coordination challenges. Our results show that even in these controlled settings, frontier LLM agents struggle to coordinate, largely due to limited understanding of the coordination problem and weak reasoning about their partner's beliefs. While LLMs introduce semantic information as an additional axis for coordination, they nonetheless fail to exploit this structure effectively. Towards this, we propose Coordination-friendly definitions (CFDs) as a principled approach for enabling robust coordination among LLM agents. Finally, we show that CFDs can be discovered automatically, removing the need for manual engineering. Code is available at https://github.com/ahayler/zsc-llm-agents.
case_studies.summary: Zero-shot coordination (ZSC) research shows that large language model (LLM) agents struggle to coordinate without shared design or training, even in simple tasks. The authors created minimal test environments and a new method called Coordination-friendly Definitions (CFDs), which can automatically be discovered to improve coordination. The result is a proof‑of‑concept that CFD‑enhanced LLM agents can coordinate better than baseline LLMs, but the gains are modest and limited to controlled settings.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, this is not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper investigates coordination among LLM agents, a topic with limited direct applicability to day‑to‑day infrastructure tasks. The authors provide code, indicating some practical implementation, but the concepts remain largely experimental and lack immediate deployment value for IT engineers. Monetisation potential is low as the work does not present a ready‑to‑sell solution or clear serviceable product. Overall impact, maturity, and monetisation are modest.
